title: Ivo and the Harbor
premise: In the coastal town of Vellamare, Sebastian Oyelaran, a mapmaker's apprentice of ambiguous origins, has spent twenty years completing the harbor atlas their murdered master died protecting—an atlas whose final pages contain the true names and hiding places of families erased by an old purge. When the army requisitions the town and seizes the master's ledgers to hunt those same families, Sebastian must choose between the silence that has kept them safe and a peacetime promise made to Ilse Marchetti, a childhood friend now declared enemy and returning in secret for her own name. As Captain Rennick closes in on both the atlas and the harbor's hidden families, Sebastian finishes the map not as a record of erasure but as a testimony, smuggling the truth out through the tide channels only they know. The book ends with Sebastian surrendering themselves to save Ilse's family, trading their invisibility for the public declaration of every name—finding identity at last, at the cost of the safety they spent a lifetime building.
about_author: A. M. Quintana is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing confiscated municipal records from port towns, work that seeded this novel's obsession with what paperwork remembers and what people survive. They live near a working harbor and write at dawn, when the fog still owns the water.

chapters.title: The Ink That Outlived Him
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. Twenty years after Master Aldous Oyelaran's execution, Sebastian inks the atlas's final plate in the ruined maproom above the harbor, keeping the shop open out of habit more than hope. The emotional beat is quiet devotion shadowed by fear: the last pages hold names no one alive is supposed to remember.

chapters.title: Requisition
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. Soldiers arrive under Captain Rennick, who announces the army now owns the town, its records, and its memory; the ledgers are seized within hours. Sebastian watches the crates leave and realizes the atlas's companion volumes—the ones with the names—are gone. The beat is dread disguised as compliance.

chapters.title: What the Ledgers Say
chapters.summary: Rennick's POV. The captain reads the confiscated ledgers and finds gaps where names should be—Aldous cut them out before his arrest. He suspects the apprentice knows where the truth went. The beat is cold, methodical menace: Rennick doesn't rage; he schedules.

chapters.title: A Promise Made in Peacetime
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV, braided with flashback. A memory surfaces of twelve-year-old Sebastian and Ilse Marchetti sealing a promise over the unfinished atlas: whoever finished it would finish it for both of them. Present-day Sebastian understands the promise has become a debt the army intends to collect. The beat is tender and foreboding.

chapters.title: The Tide Channels
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. Sebastian surveys the harbor's unmapped channels at low tide, the routes only Aldous ever charted, confirming they could move people or papers unseen. First contact: a chalk mark on the customs house door, old code, freshly drawn. The beat is awakening—silence cracking into action.

chapters.title: Enemy Waters
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV. Ilse returns by fishing boat under a false manifest, having spent years abroad learning what happened to the families the purge erased—including her own mother's name, which exists nowhere but in Aldous's stolen plates. The beat is homecoming sharpened into purpose.

chapters.title: Two Maps, One Truth
chapters.summary: Sebastian and Ilse reunite in the maproom, suspicion dissolving into shared grief and shared plan: the atlas's final plates are the only record of the erased, and Rennick holds the key to reading them. The beat is rekindled trust—and the first admission that love and duty point different directions.

chapters.title: The Apprentice's Silence
chapters.summary: Rennick's POV. Rennick summons Sebastian for a courteous interrogation, offering protection in exchange for cooperation, revealing he knows about the chalk mark. Sebastian lies well—twenty years of practice—but leaves shaken, understanding the net is already drawn. The beat is terror managed into performance.

chapters.title: Names Without Owners
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV. Ilse works the harbor's taverns and fish markets, finding survivors of the purge who have lived under borrowed names so long they flinch at their own. Some beg her to stop digging; one gives her a fragment of a stolen plate. The beat is the cost of remembrance.

chapters.title: The Copyist's Dilemma
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. Sebastian begins secretly copying the atlas's true plates onto treated sailcloth that can be rolled inside a spar, knowing each hour of copying is an hour Rennick could walk in. The beat is claustrophobic resolve—love expressed as cartography.

chapters.title: An Old Debt Called In
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. The harbormaster, who once betrayed Aldous to save his own sons, warns Sebastian that Rennick has hired a reader who can reconstruct the cut names from ink impressions. Sebastian must decide whether to hate him or use him. The beat is moral compromise offered as salvation.

chapters.title: What Loyalty Weighs
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV. Ilse confronts the harbormaster's sons, now grown soldiers in Rennick's garrison, testing whether blood loyalty can be turned against duty. One wavers; one reports the meeting. The beat is hope that curdles into exposure.

chapters.title: Midnight Survey
chapters.summary: Sebastian and Ilse alternate POV. Together they run the tide channels at night, moving the copied plates toward a waiting smuggler, nearly caught when a patrol lamp sweeps the shallows. The beat is breathless intimacy—two people made honest by danger.

chapters.title: The Reader Arrives
chapters.summary: Rennick's POV. The ink-reader reconstructs three names from the mutilated ledgers, including Ilse's mother's, and Rennick sets a trap: announce publicly that the 'Marchetti daughter' is in the town and watch who moves. The beat is the trap closing without a sound.

chapters.title: Chalk on Every Door
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. Rennick's proclamation goes up; that night, someone marks half the doors in town with the old purge symbol in solidarity or defiance—no one admits to it. Rennick orders house searches. The beat is a town discovering it was never as silent as it believed.

chapters.title: The Search
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. Soldiers tear apart the maproom while Sebastian stands aside, heart hammering over the false wall where the original plates hide behind Aldous's memorial portrait. They find nothing—but Rennick lingers, looking at Sebastian, and says he will return. The beat is survival that feels like postponement.

chapters.title: Run the Channels Alone
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV. With the garrison watching Sebastian, Ilse attempts the final channel run alone and is taken at the customs house—deliberately, Sebastian later realizes, to draw the search away from the maproom. The beat is sacrifice reframing everything.

chapters.title: Terms
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Rennick offers Sebastian the trade: the original plates and the names of every hidden family in exchange for Ilse's release and safe passage. Sebastian asks for one night to decide. The beat is the novel's moral hinge—duty to the dead versus love for the living.

chapters.title: The Finished Atlas
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. Alone at night, Sebastian completes the atlas—not the version Rennick wants, but a testimony: every restored name, every erased family, every date of the purge, bound in the master's style. Then Sebastian burns the false plates and prepares the true copy for the sea. The beat is grief transfigured into authorship.

chapters.title: What the Tide Carries
chapters.summary: Multi-POV climax. At dawn, Sebastian triggers the harbormaster's old guilt to open the customs gate, runs the channels one last time, and puts the testimony aboard the smuggler as Rennick's men close in. Caught on the quay, Sebastian chooses capture over letting the boat turn back. The beat is the promise kept at maximum price.

chapters.title: Every Name Aloud
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. In the customs hall, rather than confess quietly, Sebastian reads the restored names aloud before the assembled town—claiming their own erased name among them for the first time. Rennick, facing a crowd that now knows what its ledgers hid, cannot make the arrest look like justice. The beat is identity claimed in public, at last.

chapters.title: Ivo and the Harbor
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Ilse's POV. Months later, the testimony has reached the capital; Rennick is recalled under inquiry, and the atlas is printed under both masters' names—Aldous's and Sebastian's. Ilse finds Sebastian mapping the tide channels again, this time openly, and the harbor lights come on one by one. The beat is peace earned, not granted.
